source.title: SGEM: stochastic gradient with energy and momentum

record.tranche_reason: Compares a new adaptive optimizer with SGDM and other optimizers on held-out accuracy, using a different optimizer and benchmark setup from the version’s cited studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer comparisons on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. Its CIFAR-100 accuracy values are shown only in figures; text gives the direction of the comparison. It does not report random-label fitting, interpolation-threshold sweeps, or measurements of the training–test gap itself.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out image-classification accuracy under adaptive optimizers and momentum SGD with limited learning-rate tuning. These results bear on V4, although the proposed optimizer's success does not refute an 'often' claim about adaptive methods.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that SGEM converges faster than AEGD and generalizes better than or comparably to SGDM on the tested benchmarks.
record.recipe_differences: SGEM is a new energy-and-momentum optimizer; experiments compare it with SGDM, AEGD, and selected adaptive methods. Only the base learning rate is tuned for each method, with other adaptive-method hyperparameters at literature defaults.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture: CIFAR-100 results favor SGEM and AEGD over other methods, while ImageNet results show SGEM comparable to SGDM.
record.problems: CIFAR-100 test-accuracy values are only available in figures; the text gives no uncertainty estimates. The optimizer comparison tunes only the base learning rate and uses default settings for other adaptive-method hyperparameters.
record.rows_left_out: No reported claim-relevant results left out. Figure-only CIFAR-100 values are retained as directional results because the text explicitly describes their outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
Width-dependent generalization beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Language benchmarks, broader hyperparameter tuning, Adam-to-SGD switching, and decoupled weight decay. Better or equal training performance accompanying worse held-out performance is not established by the supplied text.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations that remove large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions and their interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Separate Adam and other conventional adaptive-optimizer comparisons against SGDM. The existing rows capture energy-method successes but omit whether the conventional adaptive methods show V4's disadvantage. Their relative ordering cannot be determined from the supplied figure text.
missing.locator: Section 5, Figure 3 test-accuracy panels and Figure 4 Adam-versus-SGDM test-accuracy curves

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Only base learning rates are tuned, with a shared decay schedule and other adaptive hyperparameters at literature defaults. The supplied text contains no readable numerical CIFAR-100 curves or uncertainty estimates; the statement about existing ImageNet experiments is background, not an additional result.

rows.subject: ResNet-18

rows.note: SGEM is described as achieving comparable test accuracy to SGDM by the end of training.
rows.check: The authors describe comparable accuracy, so the adaptive-method disadvantage is absent. The values 69.89% for SGDM and 69.92% for SGEM are highest achieved test accuracies, not explicitly final-epoch accuracies; the 0.03 percentage-point difference is not established as a meaningful advantage.
